title: Correction Experiences on Social Media During COVID-19
screen_reason: National quota survey of US adults (Lucid, 27-28 March 2020, N = 1,043 regular social media users after weighting and filtering). The paper's stated aim is correction experiences, which are out of scope, but the contextual items give two in-scope self-reported shares: seeing someone share COVID-19 misinformation on social media in the past week (56.6%) and having shared misinformation oneself in the past week (11.9%). Both are RECALL with a population denominator.

estimates.platform: social media (platform not specified in the item)
estimates.measure_type: % of US adult social media users who report seeing someone else share COVID-19 misinformation on social media in the past week
estimates.value_raw: 56.6% (N = 588 of the analysis sample of 1,043 regular social media users)
estimates.denominator: 1,043 weighted US adult respondents who report regularly using at least one social media site (Lucid Academic quota sample, raked to census/Gallup/GSS targets)
estimates.definition: Answered yes to having experienced, on social media in relation to COVID-19 in the past week, 'seeing someone else sharing misinformation'
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition given to respondents; the authors note that "whether a participant reports witnessing misinformation or correction is dependent upon their definition of those concepts"
estimates.source_quote: Just over half of participants reported seeing misinformation about COVID- 19 on social media in the past week (56.6%)
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Experiencing Correction on Social Media', p. 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Single binary self-report item (yes/no), respondent-defined misinformation, one-week recall window; the authors state they cannot know whether what respondents saw was actually false
estimates.moderator_quote: Participants were asked in the past week whether (yes or no) they had experienced any of the following on social media as related to COVID-19: (a) seeing someone else sharing misinformation, (b) sharing misinformation yourself, (c) being told you shared misinformation ("being corrected"), (d) seeing someone else being told they shared misinformation ("witnessing correction"), or (e) telling someone they shared misinformation ("correcting someone else").
estimates.notes: The subsample used in the regressions (N = 588, those who saw misinformation) is consistent with 56.6% of the 1,043-person analysis sample after listwise deletion. The sample is quota-recruited and weighted but the authors state plainly it is not representative.

estimates.platform: social media (platform not specified in the item)
estimates.measure_type: % of US adult social media users who report having shared COVID-19 misinformation themselves on social media in the past week
estimates.value_raw: 11.9% (N = 124 of the analysis sample of 1,043; reported as 12.0% and N = 136 elsewhere in the paper)
estimates.denominator: 1,043 weighted US adult respondents who report regularly using at least one social media site
estimates.definition: Answered yes to having, on social media in relation to COVID-19 in the past week, shared misinformation oneself
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition given to respondents; respondent-defined
estimates.source_quote: observe that nearly equal percentages report having shared misinformation themselves in the past week (11.9%) and having been corrected (10.3%).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Experiencing Correction on Social Media', p. 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Single binary self-report item (yes/no), respondent-defined misinformation, one-week recall window
estimates.moderator_quote: Because some people likely shared misinformation without realizing they did so (and therefore would not report it in our survey), and some people may not want to admit sharing misinformation, 11.9% is almost certainly lower than the actual percentage of people sharing misinformation
estimates.notes: This is self-reported sharing (RECALL/sharing), not behavioural sharing data. The authors themselves argue the figure understates real sharing, because people who are never corrected may not know they shared misinformation. The paper reports 11.9% (N = 124) in the results and 12.0% (N = 136) in footnote 4, an internal inconsistency worth flagging; the 11.9% figure with N = 124 is the one tied to the regression sample.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, because they measure correction experiences rather than misinformation exposure or sharing: witnessing someone being corrected (34.1% of all respondents; 51.3% of those who saw misinformation), correcting someone else (22.3%; 35.1% of those who saw misinformation), being corrected oneself (10.3%; 50.7% of those who said they shared misinformation; 4.9% among the 88.1% who said they did not). All demographic and information-source predictors (odds ratios in Table 1) and the misperception models (Table 2) are associations, not shares. Worth a human's attention: the two extracted shares rest on single binary self-report items with no definition of misinformation supplied to respondents, and the authors flag that they cannot verify that what respondents saw or shared was actually false. The 11.9% vs 12.0% discrepancy (N = 124 vs N = 136) between the results section and footnote 4 is unexplained in the text.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey of US adults fielded 27-28 March 2020 through Lucid Academic, a quota-sampled online panel (screening plus quotas on age, race, ethnicity, education, income, party, region); 1,094 participants, weighted by age, race, gender, education, partisanship and ideology with raking weights (untrimmed, range 0.27-6.75), giving N = 1,071, then restricted to regular social media users (N = 1,043) with listwise deletion. Exposure, sharing and correction each measured with a single binary past-week self-report item; no definition of misinformation provided and no validation of reported experiences. Authors note the sample is not representative and the design is cross-sectional.
rob.item6_quote: Participants were asked in the past week whether (yes or no) they had experienced any of the following on social media as related to COVID-19: (a)Bode and Vraga 5 seeing someone else sharing misinformation, (b) sharing misinformation yourself, (c) being told you shared misinformation ("being corrected"), (d) seeing someone else being told they shared misinformation ("witnessing correction"), or (e) telling someone they shared misinformation ("correcting someone else").
rob.item10_quote: Just over half of participants reported seeing misinformation about COVID- 19 on social media in the past week (56.6%), while a third reported witnessing someone else being corrected (34.1%).
